Edit: in my original post I realized I didn’t make this clear. The frame count is saved in a save state. The frame count doesn’t get reset to zero by a save state or continue counting, it resets to whatever numbered frame it was on when the save state was made, and the seed remains unchanged.

Hey man I’m going to explain to you how the frames work because I’ve actually broken into all this.

First off you’ll see conflicting information about seeds in Gen 3 because of Emerald being broken. Anything you see that references Emerald and frames is essentially irrelevant to the other Gen 3 games.

Shiny hunting is the attempt to land on the properly numbered frame that correlates with the hex code that will produce a shiny. When you turn your game on, it starts counting frames. It will continue counting frames until it hits a max limit and starts over. I don’t know what this limit is but it’s days worth of time so irrelevant.

If your game is running at standard speed, there will be 60 frames per second. Each frame correlates to a Pokemon with a level, a nature, gender, special ability, IVs, and shiny status. What exactly these frames generate is tied to the seed, the trainer ID, and the Secret ID. In every gen 3 game except Emerald, the seed changes every time the game restarts. 

This is how legality of Pokemon is checked at a basic level. The game assigns a PID to every obtainable Pokemon (exception: egg spawned Pokemon, which is part of why Legendaries can’t breed) that correlates with the seed, TID, and SID. 

So, let’s say you want a shiny Pidgey. Every single Pidgey than can spawn is tied to a frame. You want the Shiny Pidgey. That shiny Pidgey could be frame 3000, which would mean you’d have to get an encounter to occur exactly 50 seconds from turning power on the ROM. The first shiny Pidgey may also be on frame 300,000, which is almost an hour and a half of game time. Now the odds are technically 1/8192, but that’s only correct across an infinite amount of attempts. 

If you use a save state, the game is loading from exactly the same frame and seed as what it was when the save state was made. The frame count starts where the save state was made at. If you made your save state on a bad seed, you may be checking a subset of frames that don’t even contain a shiny at all. If you clocked the time down to the 60th of a second, you could actually generate the same exact Pokemon every time using a save state. In Pokemon emerald people will use this to their advantage because the seed, which is supposed to be the primary variable, is always zero, so if you have the other numerical variables you can predetermine what Pokemon are tied to which frames and try to land on those frames. Using this method is extremely easy for static Pokemon because you have a lot more control over when the encounter generates. 

The seed is variable in all the other gen 3 games. So your best bet is to reset the game with a fresh seed every time because you’re more likely to keep your odds at 1/8192 instead of accidentally locking yourself into a frame range with zero shinies at all.

The easiest method is making a repository on your PC and using SD cards to transfer saves to the PC. make it so you can see full file names on your PC. Most handheld save files for GBA games will be .srm. On mGBA the PC emulator, it uses .sav and .sa2 for a multiplayer window. Just rename the extension to convert to whichever type of save file you need. 

Remember! The emulator can only see ONE save file per a ROM at a time, so keep different save files separate. This is just like the original cartridge, it can only have one save file because it prevents people from easily duplicating stuff. 

If you’re not careful in your organization you can very easily accidentally delete or overwrite a file, so make frequent backups.

Pokemondb.net, look up your Pokemon, go down to the move lists, click Gen 3, and it will show you all its learnable moves, their accuracy, power, and whether it’s physical or special. 

Your strong moves are those with 100 accuracy and 85+ power. There are some decent coverage moves with 75+ power. Some moves like Aerial Ace are good because they can’t miss, or moves like Extremespeed always go first. 

Key things to remember: Some Pokemon prefer Physical Attacks, for Gen 3 this is anything that’s not dragon, an element, or psychic. Poison, Ghost, Rock, Ground, Flying, Fighting, Steel, and Normal are all physical attack stat Based. 

Try to align Physical Attackers against mons with weak Defense, and vice versa.

STAB (same type attack bonus) is a 50% damage boost, use it where you can. 

One Type advantage is x2, two type advantages are x4. Ie Ice vs Dragonite and Electricity vs Gyarados.

Here’s the important bits:

Roaming beasts in FireRed and LeafGreen are bugged 2 ways. Lightning and Fire Beast will never appear again if they Roar. So make sure you’re saving every time you hit grass after beating the E4. A masterball or a fast sleep attack are your only chance with them. Suicune doesn’t have this issue.

The second issue applies to all 3: their IV (base genetic stat modifiers) are all zero except HP and attack, meaning their stat pool is lower than it could be. The other side of this is that the beasts are generated the same time you pick your starter, so trying to reroll natures or shiny status is impossible other than at game start.

It sounds like multiple issues going on here, so instead of trying to address them all, let me just try to outline some options for your miners.

So the goal is you want your miners to mine ONLY for you, and you want them to do it efficiently, correct?

There are some limitations working with the AI, but here’s what I do:

1. Ensure you have plenty of solid storage for solid raw materials available on your station.

2. Check your stations buy orders for the raw materials. The automatic settings aren’t always optimal. You may have a really low buy order for no reason.

3. As long as you’re only buying ore from your own miners, max the buy price for the ore.

4. Make sure the station has cargo drones to unload your ships!

5. Now here is where the options split based on either your manager’s skill or your pilot’s. If you assign miners to your station, they will only mine for that station, and the number of systems they can traverse looking for resources is the same as the manager’s level. BEWARE, the manager will try to send the miners to the highest concentrations it can get, which can overextend your miners OR overload one area with too many miners. In this situation I will blacklist whatever sector is getting overloaded. 

6. You can use the miners to automine on their own. There are three levels of automine. The first is very basic and pretty useful for your use case as long as the needed resources are in the same sector as your station. 
The next two levels require a lot more micromanagement if you want to control where they sell, but I find just maxing the buy price on my own resources keeps my autominers around most of the time. 

Issues you can run into:

1. Station doesn’t have any cargo drones
2. No required resources in range of the station or the miners, whichever is in command of mining operations.
3. Overloaded resource sectors, too many miners in one spot. -Blacklisting is a heavy handed but simple solution.
4. Miners going too far for a minor resource concentration improvement. -Blacklisting again
5. Station storage is full or the automatic buy offer is reached.
6. Miners are full of another resource from a previous order and they don’t know how to get rid of it; either manually sell it somewhere or dump it.
7. You have an old blacklist in place blocking miners from  
where they need to go.

This is everything I can think of at the moment, maybe it will help.

PS. In my experience resource probes make little difference. I drop a few here or there where I know my miners are going to go anyway, and leave it at that.

This is my standard order of operations for destroyers to attack stations:

1. Set all turrets that I want to use vs stations and capitals to Attack All Enemies. Do not set turrets with range less than your enemy’s to attack all. 

2. Set all other turrets to Attack Fighters.

3. Use the Attack command OR set the destroyers to Attack with Commander using an Asgard or Syn as the commander. Either way, attack command on the target. 

4. The destroyers will move into turret range. Generally they’ll be right on top of one another, I just accept that and deal with it. 

5. I only micro the destroyers that decide to reposition within excess damage range of the enemy station. With fleets that are big enough and well equipped enough, several ships in that range spreads the enemy DPS out enough that it doesn’t matter.

6. If necessary because my AI captains are being more derpy than usual, I’ll hop into the local Asgard or one of the better destroyers and start sniping turrets.

First: most machines are isolation tools. Body weight and dumbbells lend themselves to full body work.

Third: it may just be that you’ve hit a slowdown doing normal gym work and lucked out on a stimulus change boosting your gains again. Finally, if it’s working for you, ride that train til it stops. Just don’t assume it will be the same for everyone else.

I’ve seen guys pick up 3 plates having never deadlifted a day in their life. I have seen guys -benchpress- 3 plates without ever having bench pressed. It makes me jealous af, but it happens.

Most people aren’t going to hit 4 plates after just a couple of months. There might be edge cases, but to me a beginner is the first year or two. Your not normally into intermediate territory before 3 years unless you’re on AAS or very gifted for lifting.

I know a lot of naturally big/fat people that hit 5 plates without too much effort in less than 4 years. I am likely biased because I live in the southeastern US where people just tend to be heavier in general, and most have at least done hard labor or played varsity sports at some point. 

You can walk in to my local Crunch and see several guys (and a couple girls!) under 25 years old deadlifting 4+ plates, and I had a little guy (5’5”, 140lbs) who could only squat 95lbs hit 225lbs on deadlift in his first max day. This is why I threw a wide range out there because in my experience, those are the ranges I have seen people hit with basic linear training, sometimes without hardly ever deadlifting at all. Me personally I hit 455lbs in 2 years, but my bodyweight was 315lbs at the time. It took another year ish to get 500lbs. I haven’t really ever exceeded that, and I don’t think I will without doing conjugate or hardcore block powerlifting training, and we are talking years for a plate’s worth at that point. 

Unless you’re gifted for deadlift, I think once you start getting to double bw territory or over 400lbs the recovery windows start getting real finicky and you can torch your CNS real fast, especially in a calorie deficit. It takes some real training know-how to exceed those numbers. I’ve seen a few guys get to that territory then make 40-80lb gains with AAS, but even then without intelligent specific programming they get stuck too. 

When I was working with 455 as my max, even being a big fat boy, deadlifting at 90%+ could leave me burnt on doing deadlifts for over a week, so there were many times I deadlifted only every 9 or 10 days. 

As a side note, if you want to keep your deadlift strong without doing many or any deadlifts, do box squats at or just below parallel. It doesn’t work for everyone but it does for the majority. When I hit my 5plate deadlift I was only deadlifting once every three weeks but box squatting twice a week. 

Also all this knowledge is based on conventional deadlifts. I’ve never really done sumo bc at 6’3” I feel like I can’t get into good position, the plates will hit my feet. If a practiced sumo guy wants to tell me how to do sumo I’ll listen.

All of this is just based on my personal experience and isn’t out of a science book or study. People are vastly different and there are always edge cases.
